title: How robust are linear-probe jailbreak detectors to simple paraphrasing and synonym substitution?

original_idea.quick_reasoning: Clearly addresses an AI Safety problem with a reasonably scoped approach.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: if linear probes fail against simple paraphrasing (no GPU-intensive optimization needed), their production value is much lower than claimed. This directly tests a minimum robustness bar for the 'almost free' detection claim. Sets actionable expectations for practitioners.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Train logistic regression on hidden states (standard sklearn workflow), generate paraphrases via LLM API, test recall. All components are well-documented and accessible. A motivated beginner can execute this with basic Python/ML skills and an LLM API key.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Tightly scoped: train one probe, generate paraphrased variants, measure recall drop. Single precise experiment with well-defined success criteria (recall at different perturbation levels) and an obvious deliverable (robustness curve). Can go from start to result quickly.

novelty.reasoning: The robustness of probe-based jailbreak detectors to perturbations has been partially studied. 'What Features in Prompts Jailbreak LLMs?' (BlackboxNLP 2025) showed linear probes have limited cross-attack generalization. PromptScreen (arXiv:2512.19011) evaluated word-level models against paraphrasing and found early saturation and robustness limitations. SemanticSmooth uses paraphrasing defensively. However, the specific experiment — training a linear probe on activation representations and systematically measuring recall drop under controlled paraphrasing perturbation levels with a robustness curve — is a focused contribution not directly replicated. The general finding (probes struggle with perturbations) is known; the systematic quantification is partially novel.
